entries.1c8338dddb5757186968c181e238aad91fa752ed: <div sID="gen11400" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="55" osisID="Ps.55" sID="Ps.55"/> <div eID="gen11400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11401" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11402" type="x-p"/> It is the conjecture of many expositors that David penned this psalm upon occasion of Absalom's rebellion, and that the particular enemy he here speaks of, that dealt treacherously with him, was Ahithophel; and some will therefore make David's troubles here typical of Christ's sufferings, and Ahithophel's treachery a figure of Judas's, because they both hanged themselves. But there is nothing in it particularly applied to Christ in the New Testament. David was in great distress when he penned this psalm. I. He prays that God would manifest his favour to him, and pleads his own sorrow and fear, <reference osisRef="Ps.56.1-Ps.56.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. He prays that God would manifest his displeasure against his enemies, and pleads their great wickedness and treachery, <reference osisRef="Ps.56.9-Ps.56.15 Ps.56.20 Ps.56.21">ver. 9-15 and again ver. 20, 21</reference>. III. He assures himself that God would, in due time, appear for him against his enemies, comforts himself with the hopes of it, and encourages others to trust in God, <reference osisRef="Ps.56.16-Ps.56.19 Ps.56.22 Ps.56.23">ver. 16-19 and again ver. 22, 23</reference>. In singing this psalm we may, if there be occasion, apply it to our own troubles; if not, we may sympathize with those to whose case it comes nearer, foreseeing that there will be, at last, indignation and wrath to the persecutors, salvation and joy to the persecuted.
entries.e172f22176e159c047c7b494ed5ffabff9818ecb: <div eID="gen11402" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11401" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Supplications of David in Distress.</title> <div sID="gen11403" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Give ear to my prayer, O God; and hide not thyself from my supplication. <hi type="super">2</hi> Attend unto me, and hear me: I mourn in my complaint, and make a noise; <hi type="super">3</hi> Because of the voice of the enemy, because of the oppression of the wicked: for they cast iniquity upon me, and in wrath they hate me. <hi type="super">4</hi> My heart is sore pained within me: and the terrors of death are fallen upon me. <hi type="super">5</hi> Fearfulness and trembling are come upon me, and horror hath overwhelmed me. <hi type="super">6</hi> And I said, Oh that I had wings like a dove! <hi type="italic">for then</hi> would I fly away, and be at rest. <hi type="super">7</hi> Lo, <hi type="italic">then</hi> would I wander far off, <hi type="italic">and</hi> remain in the wilderness. Selah. <hi type="super">8</hi> I would hasten my escape from the windy storm <hi type="italic">and</hi> tempest. <div eID="gen11403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11404" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen11404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11405" type="x-p"/> I. David praying. Prayer is a salve for every sore and a relief to the spirit under every burden: <hi type="italic">Give ear to my prayer, O God!</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.55.1-Ps.55.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. He does not set down the petitions he offered up to God in his distress, but begs that God would hear the prayers which, at every period, his heart lifted up to God, and grant an answer of peace to them: <hi type="italic">Attend to me, hear me.</hi> Saul would not hear his petitions; his other enemies regarded not his pleas; but, "Lord, be thou pleased to hearken to me. <hi type="italic">Hide not thyself from my supplication,</hi> either as one unconcerned and not regarding it, nor seeming to take any notice of it, or as one displeased, angry at me, and therefore at my prayer." If we, in our prayers, sincerely lay open ourselves, our case, our hearts, to God, we have reason to hope that he will not hide himself, his favours, his comforts, from us. <div eID="gen11405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11406" type="x-p"/> II. David weeping; for in this he was a type of Christ that he was a man of sorrows and often in tears (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I mourn in my complaint</hi>" (or in my <hi type="italic">meditation,</hi> my <hi type="italic">melancholy musings</hi>), "and I make a noise; I cannot forbear such sighs and groans, and other expressions of grief, as discover it to those about me." Great griefs are sometimes noisy and clamorous, and thus are, in some measure, lessened, while those increase that are stifled, and have no vent given them. But what was the matter? <reference osisRef="Ps.55.3">v. 3</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">because of the voice of the enemy,</hi> the menaces and insults of Absalom's party, that swelled, and hectored, and stirred up the people to cry out against David, and shout him out of his palace and capital city, as afterwards the chief priests stirred up the mob to cry out against the Son of David, <hi type="italic">Away with him—Crucify him.</hi> Yet it was not the voice of the enemy only that fetched tears from David's eyes, but their oppression, and the hardship he was thereby reduced to: <hi type="italic">They cast iniquity upon me.</hi> They could not justly charge David with any mal-administration in his government, could not prove any act of oppression or injustice upon him, but they loaded him with calumnies. Though they found no iniquity in him relating to his trust as a king, yet they cast all manner of iniquity upon him, and represented him to the people as a tyrant fit to be expelled. Innocency itself is no security against violent and lying tongues. They hated him themselves, nay, in wrath they hated him; there was in their enmity both the heat and violence of anger, or sudden passion, and the implacableness of hatred and rooted malice; and therefore they studied to make him odious, that others also might hate him. This made him mourn, and the more because he could remember the time when he was the darling of the people, and answered to his name, <hi type="italic">David</hi>—<hi type="italic">a beloved one.</hi> <div eID="gen11406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11407" type="x-p"/> III. David trembling, and in great consternation. We may well suppose him to be so upon the breaking out of Absalom's conspiracy and the general defection of the people, even those that he had little reason to suspect. 1. See what fear seized him. David was a man of great boldness, and in some very eminent instances had signalized his courage, and yet, when the danger was surprising and imminent, his heart failed him. Let not the stout man therefore glory in his courage any more than the strong man in his strength. Now David's <hi type="italic">heart is sorely pained within him; the terrors of death have fallen upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.55.4">v. 4</reference>. Fearfulness of mind and trembling of body came upon him, and horror covered and overwhelmed him, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.5">v. 5</reference>. When without are fightings no marvel that within are fears; and, if it was upon the occasion of Absalom's rebellion, we may suppose that the remembrance of his sin in the matter of Uriah, which God was now reckoning with him for, added as much more to the fright. Sometimes David's faith made him, in a manner, fearless, and he could boldly say, when surrounded with enemies, <hi type="italic">I will not be afraid what man can do unto me.</hi> But at other times his fears prevail and tyrannise; for the best men are not always alike strong in faith. 2. See how desirous he was, in this fright, to retire into a desert, any where to be far enough from hearing the voice of the enemy and seeing their oppressions. He said (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.6">v. 6</reference>), said it to God in prayer, said it to himself in meditation, said it to his friends in complaint, <hi type="italic">O that I had wings like a dove!</hi> Much as he had been sometimes in love with Jerusalem, now that it had become a rebellious city he longed to get clear of it, and, like the prophet, wished he had <hi type="italic">in the wilderness a lodging place of way-faring men, that he might leave his people and go from them; for they were an assembly of treacherous men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.9.2">Jer. ix. 2</reference>. This agrees very well with David's resolution upon the breaking out of that plot, <hi type="italic">Arise, let us flee, and make speed to depart,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.14">2 Sam. xv. 14</reference>. Observe, (1.) How he would make his escape. He was so surrounded with enemies that he saw not how he could escape but upon the wing, and therefore he wishes, <hi type="italic">O that I had wings!</hi> not like a hawk that flies swiftly; he wishes for wings, not to fly upon the prey, but to fly from the birds of prey, for such his enemies were. The wings of a dove were most agreeable to him who was of a dove-like spirit, and therefore the wings of an eagle would not become him. The dove flies low, and takes shelter as soon as she can, and thus would David fly. (2.) What he would make his escape from—<hi type="italic">from the wind, storm, and tempest,</hi> the tumult and ferment that the city was now in, and the danger to which he was exposed. Herein he was like a dove, that cannot endure noise. (3.) What he aimed at in making this escape, not victory but rest: "<hi type="italic">I would fly away and be at rest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.55.6">v. 6</reference>. I would fly any where, if it were to a barren frightful wilderness, ever so far off, so I might be quiet," <reference osisRef="Ps.55.7">v. 7</reference>. Note, Peace and quietness in silence and solitude are what the wisest and best of men have most earnestly coveted, and the more when they have been vexed and wearied with the noise and clamour of those about them. Gracious souls wish to retire from the hurry and bustle of this world, that they may sweetly enjoy God and themselves; and, if there be any true peace on this side heaven, it is they that enjoy it in those retirements. This makes death desirable to a child of God, that it is a final escape from all the storms and tempests of this world to perfect and everlasting rest.
entries.ade7a12bbf9e269fad46246f990f4215a0086fb4: <div eID="gen11407" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Prophetic Imprecations.</title> <div sID="gen11408" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Destroy, O Lord, <hi type="italic">and</hi> divide their tongues: for I have seen violence and strife in the city. <hi type="super">10</hi> Day and night they go about it upon the walls thereof: mischief also and sorrow <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the midst of it. <hi type="super">11</hi> Wickedness <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the midst thereof: deceit and guile depart not from her streets. <hi type="super">12</hi> For <hi type="italic">it was</hi> not an enemy <hi type="italic">that</hi> reproached me; then I could have borne <hi type="italic">it:</hi> neither <hi type="italic">was it</hi> he that hated me <hi type="italic">that</hi> did magnify <hi type="italic">himself</hi> against me; then I would have hid myself from him: <hi type="super">13</hi> But <hi type="italic">it was</hi> thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance. <hi type="super">14</hi> We took sweet counsel together, <hi type="italic">and</hi> walked unto the house of God in company. <hi type="super">15</hi> Let death seize upon them, <hi type="italic">and</hi> let them go down quick into hell: for wickedness <hi type="italic">is</hi> in their dwellings, <hi type="italic">and</hi> among them. <div eID="gen11408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11409" type="x-p"/> David here complains of his enemies, whose wicked plots had brought him, though not to his faith's end, yet to his wits' end, and prays against them by the spirit of prophecy. Observe here, <div eID="gen11409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11410" type="x-p"/> I. The character he gives of the enemies he feared. They were of the worst sort of men, and his description of them agrees very well with Absalom and his accomplices. 1. He complains of the city of Jerusalem, which strangely fell in with Absalom and fell off from David, so that he had none there but his own guards and servants that he could repose any confidence in: <hi type="italic">How has that faithful city become a harlot!</hi> David did not take the representation of it from others; but with his own eyes, and with a sad heart, did himself see nothing but <hi type="italic">violence and strife in the city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.9">v. 9</reference>); for, when they grew disaffected and disloyal to David, they grew mischievous one to another. If he walked the rounds upon the walls of the city, he saw that violence and strife went about it day and night, and mounted its guards, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.10">v. 10</reference>. All the arts and methods which the rebels used for the fortifying of the city were made up on violence and strife, and there were no remains of honesty or love among them. If he looked into the heart of the city, mischief and injury, mutual wrong and vexation, were in the midst of it: <hi type="italic">Wickedness,</hi> all manner of wickedness, <hi type="italic">is in the midst thereof. Jusque datum sceleri—Wickedness was legalized.</hi> Deceit and guile, and all manner of treacherous dealing, <hi type="italic">departed not from her streets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.55.11">v. 11</reference>. It may be meant of their base and barbarous usage of David's friends and such as they knew were firm and faithful to him; they did them all the mischief they could, by fraud or force. Is this the character of Jerusalem, the royal city, and, which is more, the holy city, and in David's time too, so soon after the thrones of judgment and the testimony of Israel were both placed there? <hi type="italic">Is this the city that men call the perfection of beauty?</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">Lam. ii. 15</reference>. Is Jerusalem, the head-quarters of God's priests, so ill taught? Can Jerusalem be ungrateful to David himself, its own illustrious founder, and be made too hot for him, so that he cannot reside in it? Let us not be surprised at the corruptions and disorders of this church on earth, but long to see the New Jerusalem, where there is no violence nor strife, no mischief nor guilt, and into which no unclean thing shall enter, nor any thing that disquiets. 2. He complains of one of the ringleaders of the conspiracy, that had been very industrious to foment jealousies, to misrepresent him and his government, and to incense the city against him. It was one that reproached him, as if he either abused his power or neglected the use of it, for that was Absalom's malicious suggestion: <hi type="italic">There is no man deputed of the king to hear thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.3">2 Sam. xv. 3</reference>. That and similar accusations were industriously spread among the people; and who was most active in it? "Not a sworn enemy, not Shimei, nor any of the nonjurors; then I could have borne it, for I should not have expected better from them" (and we find how patiently he did bear Shimei's curses); "not one that professed to hate me, then I would have stood upon my guard against him, would have hidden myself and counsels from him, so that it would not have been in his power to betray me. <hi type="italic">But it was thou, a man, my equal,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.55.13">v. 13</reference>. The Chaldee-paraphrase names Ahithophel as the person here meant, and nothing in that plot seems to have discouraged David so much as to hear that Ahithophel was <hi type="italic">among the conspirators with Absalom</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.31">2 Sam. xv. 31</reference>), for he was <hi type="italic">the king's counsellor,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.33">1 Chron. xxvii. 33</reference>. "<hi type="italic">It was thou, a man, my equal,</hi> one whom I esteemed as myself, a friend as my own soul, whom I had laid in my bosom and made equal with myself, to whom I had communicated all my secrets and who knew my mind as well as I myself did,—my guide, with whom I advised and by whom I was directed in all my affairs, whom I made president of the council and prime-minister of state,—my intimate acquaintance and familiar friend; this is the man that now abuses me. I have been kind to him, but I find him thus basely ungrateful. I have put a trust in him, but I find him thus basely treacherous; nay, and he could not have done me the one-half of the mischief he does if I had not shown him so much respect." All this must needs be very grievous to an ingenuous mind, and yet this was not all; this traitor had seemed a saint, else he had never been David's bosom-friend (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">We took counsel together,</hi> spent many an hour together, with a great deal of pleasure, in religious discourse," or, as Dr. Hammond reads it, "<hi type="italic">We joined ourselves together to the assembly;</hi> I gave him the right hand of fellowship in holy ordinances, and then <hi type="italic">we walked to the house of God in company,</hi> to attend the public service." Note, (1.) There always has been, and always will be, a mixture of good and bad, sound and unsound, in the visible church, between whom, perhaps for a long time, we can discern no difference; but the searcher of hearts does. David, who went to the house of God in his sincerity, had Ahithophel in company with him, who went in his hypocrisy. The Pharisee and the publican went together to the temple to pray; but, sooner or later, those that are perfect and those that are not will be made manifest. (2.) Carnal policy may carry men on very far and very long in a profession of religion while it is in fashion, and will serve a turn. In the court of pious David none was more devout than Ahithophel, and yet his heart was not right in the sight of God. (3.) We must not wonder if we be sadly deceived in some that have made great pretensions to those two sacred things, religion and friendship; David himself, though a very wise man, was thus imposed upon, which may make similar disappointments the more tolerable to us. <div eID="gen11410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11411" type="x-p"/> II. His prayers against them, which we are both to stand in awe of and to comfort ourselves in, as prophecies, but not to copy into our prayers against any particular enemies of our own. He prays, 1. That God would disperse them, as he did the Babel-builders (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Destroy, O Lord! and divide their tongues;</hi> that is, blast their counsels, by making them to disagree among themselves, and clash with one another. Send an evil spirit among them, that they may not understand one another, but be envious and jealous one of another." This prayer was answered in the turning of Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness, by setting up the counsel of Hushai against it. God often destroys the church's enemies by dividing them; nor is there a surer way to the destruction of any people than their division. A kingdom, an interest, divided against itself, cannot long stand. 2. That God would destroy them, as he did Dathan and Abiram, and their associates, who were confederate against Moses, whose throat being an open sepulchre, the earth therefore opened and swallowed them up. This was then a new thing which God executed, <reference osisRef="Num.16.30">Num. xvi. 30</reference>. But David prays that it might now be repeated, or something equivalent (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.15">v. 15</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let death seize upon them</hi> by divine warrant, and <hi type="italic">let them go down quickly into hell;</hi> let them be dead, and buried, and so utterly destroyed, in a moment; for wickedness is wherever they are; it is in the midst of them." The souls of impenitent sinners go down quick, or alive, into hell, for they have a perfect sense of their miseries, and shall <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> live still, that they may be still miserable. This prayer is a prophecy of the utter, the final, the everlasting ruin of all those who, whether secretly or openly, oppose and rebel against the Lord's Messiah.
entries.70fd1f285299c024cbc1b36c4627fa2f8e600264: <div eID="gen11411" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Confidence in God.</title> <div sID="gen11412" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> As for me, I will call upon God; and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall save me. <hi type="super">17</hi> Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice. <hi type="super">18</hi> He hath delivered my soul in peace from the battle <hi type="italic">that was</hi> against me: for there were many with me. <hi type="super">19</hi> God shall hear, and afflict them, even he that abideth of old. Selah. Because they have no changes, therefore they fear not God. <hi type="super">20</hi> He hath put forth his hands against such as be at peace with him: he hath broken his covenant. <hi type="super">21</hi> <hi type="italic">The words</hi> of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war <hi type="italic">was</hi> in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet <hi type="italic">were</hi> they drawn swords. <hi type="super">22</hi> Cast thy burden upon the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved. <hi type="super">23</hi> But thou, O God, shalt bring them down into the pit of destruction: bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days; but I will trust in thee. <div eID="gen11412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11413" type="x-p"/> In these verses, <div eID="gen11413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11414" type="x-p"/> I. David perseveres in his resolution to call upon God, being well assured that he should not seek him in vain (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">As for me,</hi> let them take what course they please to secure themselves, let violence and strife be their guards, prayer shall be mine; this I have found comfort in, and therefore this will I abide by: <hi type="italic">I will call upon God,</hi> and commit myself to him, and <hi type="italic">the Lord shall save me;</hi>" for whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord, in a right manner, shall be saved, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.13">Rom. x. 13</reference>. He resolves to be both fervent and frequent in this duty. 1. He will pray fervently: "<hi type="italic">I will pray and cry aloud. I will meditate</hi>" (so the former word signifies); "I will speak with my own heart, and the prayer shall come thence." Then we pray aright when we pray with all that is within us, think first and then pray over our thoughts; for the true nature of prayer is lifting up the heart to God. Having meditated, he will cry, he will cry aloud; the fervour of his spirit in prayer shall be expressed and yet more excited by the intenseness and earnestness of his voice. 2. He will pray frequently, every day, and three times a day—<hi type="italic">evening, and morning, and at noon.</hi> It is probable that this had been his constant practice, and he resolves to continue it now that he is in his distress. Then we may come the more boldly to the throne of grace in trouble when we do not then first begin to seek acquaintance with God, but it is what we have constantly practised, and the trouble finds the wheels of prayer going. Those that think three meals a day little enough for the body ought much more to think three solemn prayers a day little enough for the soul, and to count it a pleasure, not a task. As it is fit that in the morning we should begin the day with God, and in the evening close it with him, so it is fit that in the midst of the day we should retire awhile to converse with him. It was Daniel's practice to pray three times a day (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.10">Dan. vi. 10</reference>), and noon was one of Peter's hours of prayer, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.9">Acts x. 9</reference>. Let not us be weary of praying often, for God is not weary of hearing. "He shall hear my voice, and not blame me for coming too often, but the oftener the better, the more welcome." <div eID="gen11414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11415" type="x-p"/> II. He assures himself that God would in due time give an answer of peace to his prayers. <div eID="gen11415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11416" type="x-p"/> 1. That he himself should be delivered and his fears prevented; those fears with which he was much disordered (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.4-Ps.55.5">v. 4, 5</reference>) by the exercise of faith were now silenced, and he begins to rejoice in hope (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">God has delivered my soul in peace,</hi> that is, he will deliver it; David is as sure of the deliverance as if it were already wrought. His enemies were at war with him, and the battle was against him, but God delivered him in peace, that is, brought him off with as much comfort as if he had never been in danger. If he did not deliver him in victory, yet he delivered him in peace, inward peace. He delivered his soul in peace; by patience and holy joy in God he kept possession of that. Those are safe and easy whose hearts and minds are kept by that peace of God which <hi type="italic">passes all understanding,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.7">Phil. iv. 7</reference>. David, in his fright, thought all were against him; but now he sees there were many with him, more than he imagined; his interest proved better than he expected, and this he gives to God the glory of: for it is he that raises us up friends when we need them, and makes them faithful to us. There were many with him; for though his subjects deserted him, and went over to Absalom, yet God was with him and the good angels. With an eye of faith he now sees himself surrounded, as Elisha was, with chariots of fire and horses of fire, and therefore triumphs thus, <hi type="italic">There are many with me,</hi> more <hi type="italic">with me than against me,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.16-2Kgs.6.17">2 Kings vi. 16, 17</reference>. <div eID="gen11416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11417" type="x-p"/> 2. That his enemies should be reckoned with, and brought down. They had frightened him with their menaces (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.3">v. 3</reference>), but here he says enough to frighten them and make them tremble with more reason, and no remedy; for they could not ease themselves of their fears as David could, by faith in God. <div eID="gen11417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11418" type="x-p"/> (1.) David here gives their character as the reason why he expected God would bring them down. [1.] They are impious and profane, and stand in no awe of God, of his authority or wrath (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.19">v. 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Because they have no changes</hi> (no afflictions, no interruption to the constant course of their prosperity, no crosses to empty them from vessel to vessel) <hi type="italic">therefore they fear not God;</hi> they live in a constant neglect and contempt of God and religion, which is the cause of all their other wickedness, and by which they are certainly marked for destruction." [2.] They are treacherous and false, and will not be held by the most sacred and solemn engagements (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He has put forth his hand against such as are at peace with him,</hi> that never provoked him, nor gave him any cause to quarrel with them; nay, to whom he had given all possible encouragement to expect kindness from him. He has put forth his hand against those whom he had given his hand to, and has broken his covenant both with God and man, has perfidiously violated his engagement to both," than which nothing makes men riper for ruin. [3.] They are base and hypocritical, pretending friendship while they design mischief (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.21">v. 21</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The words of his mouth</hi>" (probably, he means Ahithophel particularly) "<hi type="italic">were smoother than butter and softer than oil,</hi> so courteous was he and obliging, so free in his professions of respect and kindness and the proffers of his service; yet, at the same time, <hi type="italic">war was in his heart,</hi> and all this courtesy was but a stratagem of war, and those very words had such a mischievous design in them that they were as <hi type="italic">drawn swords</hi> designed to stab." They smile in a man's face, and cut his throat at the same time, as Joab, that kissed and killed. Satan is such an enemy; he flatters men into their ruin. <hi type="italic">When he speaks fair, believe him not.</hi> <div eID="gen11418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11419" type="x-p"/> (2.) David here foretels their ruin. [1.] God shall afflict them, and bring them into straits and frights, and recompense tribulation to those that have troubled his people, and this in answer to the prayers of his people: <hi type="italic">God shall hear and afflict them,</hi> hear the cries of the oppressed and speak terror to their oppressors, <hi type="italic">even he that abides of old,</hi> who is God from everlasting, and world without end, and who sits Judge from the beginning of time, and has always presided in the affairs of the children of men. Mortal men, though ever so high and strong, will easily be crushed by an eternal God and are a very unequal match for him. This the saints have comforted themselves with in reference to the threatening power of the church's enemies (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.12">Hab. i. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Art thou not from everlasting, O Lord?</hi> [2.] God shall <hi type="italic">bring them down,</hi> not only to the dust, but <hi type="italic">to the pit of destruction</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.23">v. 23</reference>), to the bottomless pit, which is called <hi type="italic">destruction,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.26.6">Job xxvi. 6</reference>. He afflicted them (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.19">v. 19</reference>) to see if that would humble and reform them; but, they not being wrought upon by that, he shall at last bring them to ruin. Those that are not reclaimed by the rod of affliction will certainly be brought down into the pit of destruction. They are <hi type="italic">bloody and deceitful men</hi> (that is, the worst of men) and therefore <hi type="italic">shall not live out half their days,</hi> not half so long as men ordinarily live, and as they might have lived in a course of nature, and as they themselves expected to live. They shall live as long as the Lord of life, the righteous Judge, has appointed, with whom the number of our months is; but he has determined to cut them off by an untimely death in the midst of their days. They were bloody men, and cut others off, and therefore God will justly cut them off: they were deceitful men, and defrauded others of the one-half perhaps of what was their due, and now God will cut them short, though not of that which was their due, yet of that which they counted upon. <div eID="gen11419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11420" type="x-p"/> III. He encourages himself and all good people to commit themselves to God, with confidence in him. He himself resolves to do so (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.23">v. 23</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will trust in thee,</hi> in thy providence, and power, and mercy, and not in my own prudence, strength, or merit; when bloody and deceitful men are cut off in the midst of their days I shall still live by faith in thee." And this he will have others to do (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Cast thy burden upon the Lord,</hi>" whoever thou art that art burdened, and whatever the burden is. "<hi type="italic">Cast thy gift upon the Lord</hi>" (so some read it); "whatever blessings God has bestowed upon thee to enjoy commit them all to his custody, and particularly commit the keeping of thy soul to him." Or, "Whatever it is that thou desirest God should give thee, leave it to him to give it to thee in his own way and time. <hi type="italic">Cast thy care upon the Lord,</hi>" so the LXX., to which the apostle refers, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.7">1 Pet. v. 7</reference>. Care is a burden; it makes the heart stoop (<reference osisRef="Prov.12.25">Prov. xii. 25</reference>); we must cast it upon God by faith and prayer, commit our way and works to him; let him do as seemeth him good, and we will be satisfied. To cast our burden upon God is to stay ourselves on his providence and promise, and to be very easy in the assurance that all shall work for good. If we do so, it is promised, 1. That he will sustain us, both support and supply us, will himself carry us in the arms of his power, as the nurse carries the sucking-child, will strengthen our spirits so by his Spirit as that they shall sustain the infirmity. He has not promised to free us immediately from that trouble which gives rise to our cares and fears; but he will provide that we be not tempted above what we are able, and that we shall be able according as we are tempted. 2. That he will never suffer the righteous to be moved, to be so shaken by any troubles as to quit either their duty to God or their comfort in him. However, he will not suffer them to be moved for ever (as some read it); though they fall, they shall not be utterly cast down.  <chapter eID="Ps.55"/> <div eID="gen11420" type="x-p"/>

entries.e479b232a2057055af037e46693641bd4a5799ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6087"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 55</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.55.1-Ps.55.23">Psa 55:1-23</reference>. In great terror on account of enemies, and grieved by the treachery of a friend, the Psalmist offers an earnest prayer for relief. He mingles confident assurances of divine favor to himself with invocations and predictions of God's avenging judgments on the wicked. The tone suits David's experience, both in the times of Saul and Absalom, though perhaps neither was exclusively before his mind.</title> <div sID="gen9300" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6087"/><hi type="bold">1. hide not thyself, &c.--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Ps.13.1">Psa 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.9">27:9</reference>), withhold not help. <div eID="gen9300" type="x-p"/>
entries.6df6ee66498108cf8d39b8dd50bfcd4a29e9cfa4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6088"/><div sID="gen9301" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6088"/>2. The terms of the last clause express full indulgence of grief. <div eID="gen9301" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a598d88a293a3ed7473d8593fe6f94220269ea8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6089"/><div sID="gen9302" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6089"/><hi type="bold">3. oppression--</hi>literally, "persecution."<div eID="gen9302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9303" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they ... iniquity--</hi>literally, "they make evil doings slide upon me." <div eID="gen9303" type="x-p"/>
entries.ccb0c2eed84d9f642624ec74b2531a9134cf53e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6090"/><div sID="gen9304" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6090"/>4-5. express great alarm. <div eID="gen9304" type="x-p"/>
entries.9742761c19aa3642c362c4d78ec67f5749f4092e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6092"/><div sID="gen9306" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6092"/><hi type="bold">6. be at rest--</hi>literally, "dwell," that is, permanently. <div eID="gen9306" type="x-p"/>
entries.6113692298c804d917bcbf2f5a6e13dcf5da12ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6093"/><div sID="gen9307" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6093"/>7-8. Even a wilderness is a safer place than exposure to such evils, terrible as storm and tempest. <div eID="gen9307" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c2f3b7283c6dce7d513fadda575c1c61c1d65e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6094"/><div sID="gen9308" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6094"/><hi type="bold">9. Destroy--</hi>literally, "swallow" (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.9">Psa 21:9</reference>).<div eID="gen9308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">divide their tongues--</hi>or, "confound their speech," and hence their counsels (<reference osisRef="Gen.11.7">Ge 11:7</reference>).<div eID="gen9309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9310" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the city--</hi>perhaps Jerusalem, the scene of anarchy. <div eID="gen9310" type="x-p"/>
entries.c00374d297cc4f9d1930f0100f4bfbb836a6b5d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6095"/><div sID="gen9311" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6095"/>10-11. which is described in detail (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.7.14-Ps.7.16">Psa 7:14-16</reference>). <div eID="gen9311" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0f24f889578c9a612324588eb507ef4022aa230: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6097"/><div sID="gen9314" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6097"/>12-14. This description of treachery does not deny, but aggravates, the injury from enemies. <div eID="gen9314" type="x-p"/>
entries.9fb280e3f4e44a43c1e0ff18be51142fa7e5cc07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6100"/><div sID="gen9318" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6100"/><hi type="bold">15. Let death, &c.--</hi>or, "Desolations are on them."<div eID="gen9318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9319" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let them go--</hi>literally, "they will go."<div eID="gen9319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9320" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">quick--</hi>or, living in the midst of life, death will come (compare <reference osisRef="Num.16.33">Nu 16:33</reference>).<div eID="gen9320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9321" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among them--</hi>or, "within them," in their hearts (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.9">Psa 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.11">49:11</reference>). <div eID="gen9321" type="x-p"/>
entries.11f64bc875f2d1c75a7e8b980ee7d4ed264eed58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6101"/><div sID="gen9322" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6101"/>16-18. God answers his constant and repeated prayers. <div eID="gen9322" type="x-p"/>
entries.328486fe71267390a13571efd0d0f33350bf4960: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6103"/><div sID="gen9324" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6103"/>19. God hears the wicked in wrath.<div eID="gen9324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9325" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abideth--</hi>or, "sitteth."<div eID="gen9325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9326" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of old--</hi>enthroned as a sovereign.<div eID="gen9326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9327" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Because ... no changes--</hi>Prosperity hardens them (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.5">Psa 73:5</reference>). <div eID="gen9327" type="x-p"/>
entries.d08503df4cede703e146ee5119e8c6761fd9c397: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6104"/><div sID="gen9328" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6104"/>20-21. The treachery is aggravated by hypocrisy. The changes of number, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.15">Psa 55:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.23">23</reference>, and here, enliven the picture, and imply that the chief traitor and his accomplices are in view together. <div eID="gen9328" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7b2097d11073794f6d978ff70521be6fece7ff5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6105"/><div sID="gen9329" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6105"/><hi type="bold">22. thy burden--</hi>literally, "gift," what is assigned you.<div eID="gen9329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9330" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall sustain--</hi>literally, "supply food," and so all need (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.25">Psa 37:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.11">Mt 6:11</reference>).<div eID="gen9330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9331" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be moved--</hi>from the secure position of His favor (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.10.6">Psa 10:6</reference>). <div eID="gen9331" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a7475ef5296d6d369ddf67257fdf80672894594: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6106"/><div sID="gen9332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6106"/><hi type="bold">23. bloody ... days--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Ps.5.6">Psa 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.14">51:14</reference>), deceit and murderous dispositions often united. The threat is directed specially (not as a general truth) against the wicked, then in the writer's view. <chapter eID="Ps.55"/>

entries.a8b4489c8bc344de09107687e686fb3a80a78e7f: <div eID="gen20347" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20348" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20349" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20349" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20348" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20350" type="x-p"/> David, in great danger and distress from the implacable malice of his enemies, calls on God for mercy, <reference osisRef="Psa.55.1-Psa.55.5">Psa 55:1-5</reference>; wishes he had the wings of a dove, that he might flee away, and be at rest, <reference osisRef="Psa.55.6-Psa.55.8">Psa 55:6-8</reference>; prays against his enemies, and describes their wickedness, <reference osisRef="Psa.55.9-Psa.55.11">Psa 55:9-11</reference>; speaks of a false friend, who had been the principal cause of all his distresses, <reference osisRef="Psa.55.12-Psa.55.14">Psa 55:12-14</reference>; again prays against his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.55.15">Psa 55:15</reference>; expresses his confidence in God, <reference osisRef="Psa.55.16-Psa.55.18">Psa 55:16-18</reference>; gives a farther description of the deceitful friend, <reference osisRef="Psa.55.19-Psa.55.21">Psa 55:19-21</reference>; encourages himself in the Lord, and foretells the destruction of his foes, <reference osisRef="Psa.55.22">Psa 55:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.55.23">Psa 55:23</reference>. <div eID="gen20350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20351" type="x-p"/> The title, "To the chief Musician upon Neginoth, A Psalm of David, giving instruction." This is the same as the preceding, <reference osisRef="Psa.54.1-Psa.54.7">Psa 54:1-7</reference> (note), which see. <div eID="gen20351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20352" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20353" type="x-p"/> Give ear to my prayer - The frequency of such petitions shows the great earnestness of David's soul. If God did not hear and help, he knew he could not succeed elsewhere; therefore he continues to knock at the gate of God's mercy.
entries.640be8b0afe59e7be0b27708ab2f9c0970a3105e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20354" type="x-p"/> I mourn in my complaint - בשיחי besichi, in my sighing; a strong guttural sound, expressive of the natural accents of sorrow. <div eID="gen20354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20355" type="x-p"/> And make a noise - I am in a tumult - I am strongly agitated.
entries.6b41652f9ee8615ffbb7897188bfebda03fcb038: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20356" type="x-p"/> They cast iniquity upon me - To give a colourable pretense to their rebellion, they charge me with horrible crimes; as if they had said: Down with such a wretch; he is not fit to reign. Clamour against the person of the sovereign is always the watch-word of insurrection, in reference to rebellion.
entries.a71b2617b9bb30aa047254eac78fa9c0cc7db366: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20357" type="x-p"/> The terrors of death are fallen upon me - I am in hourly expectation of being massacred.
entries.5b3f50255fd6293f259d33581964005193c6b9f5: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20358" type="x-p"/> Fearfulness - How natural is this description! He is in distress; - he mourns; - makes a noise; - sobs and sighs; - his heart is wounded - he expects nothing but death; - this produces fear; - this produces tremor, which terminates in that deep apprehension of approaching and inevitable ruin that overwhelms him with horror. No man ever described a wounded heart like David.
entries.8d8c41fa850d48dde8c94159d650e39e7ae91505: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20359" type="x-p"/> O that I had wings like a dove! - He was so surrounded, so hemmed in on every side by his adversaries, that he could see no way for his escape unless he had wings, and could take flight. The dove is a bird of very rapid wing; and some oil them passing before his eyes at the time, might have suggested the idea expressed here. <div eID="gen20359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20360" type="x-p"/> And be at rest - Get a habitation.
entries.401b66b8dbdda74f86958fdcd0d562cee1d8e838: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20361" type="x-p"/> Would I wander far off - He did escape; and yet his enemies were so near, as to throw stones at him: but he escaped beyond Jordan. <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.22">2Sam 17:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.23">2Sam 17:23</reference>. <div eID="gen20361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20362" type="x-p"/> A passage in the Octavia of Seneca has been referred to as being parallel to this of David. It is in the answer of Octavia to the Chorus, Acts v., ver. 914-923. <div eID="gen20362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20363" type="x-p"/> Quis mea digne deflere potest Mala? <div eID="gen20363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20364" type="x-p"/> Quae lacrymis nostris quaestus <div eID="gen20364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20365" type="x-p"/> Reddet Aedon? cujus pennas <div eID="gen20365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20366" type="x-p"/> Utinam miserae mihi fata darent! <div eID="gen20366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20367" type="x-p"/> Fugerem luctus ablata meos <div eID="gen20367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20368" type="x-p"/> Penna volucri, procul et coetus <div eID="gen20368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20369" type="x-p"/> Hominum tristes sedemque feram. <div eID="gen20369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20370" type="x-p"/> Sola in vacuo nemore, et tenui <div eID="gen20370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20371" type="x-p"/> Ramo pendens, querulo possem <div eID="gen20371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20372" type="x-p"/> Gutture moestum fundere murmur. <div eID="gen20372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20373" type="x-p"/> My woes who enough can bewail? <div eID="gen20373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20374" type="x-p"/> O what notes can my sorrows express? <div eID="gen20374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20375" type="x-p"/> Sweet Philomel's self e'en would fail <div eID="gen20375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20376" type="x-p"/> To respond with her plaintive distress. <div eID="gen20376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20377" type="x-p"/> O had I her wings I would fly <div eID="gen20377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20378" type="x-p"/> To where sorrows I ne'er should feel more, <div eID="gen20378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20379" type="x-p"/> Upborne on her plumes through the sky, <div eID="gen20379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20380" type="x-p"/> Regions far from mankind would explore. <div eID="gen20380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20381" type="x-p"/> In a grove where sad silence should reign, <div eID="gen20381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20382" type="x-p"/> On a spray would I seat me alone; <div eID="gen20382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20383" type="x-p"/> In shrill lamentations complain, <div eID="gen20383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20384" type="x-p"/> And in wailings would pour forth my moan. <div eID="gen20384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20385" type="x-p"/> J. B. Clarke.
entries.bea0b3b2146539eb4d0ac830f6dced4056bbcd36: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen20385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20386" type="x-p"/> The windy storm - From the sweeping wind and tempest - Absalom and his party and the mutinous people in general.
entries.048a0971ebe455ced9bc8eeacdef7047dd030e44: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen20386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20387" type="x-p"/> Destroy, O lord - Swallow them up - confound them. <div eID="gen20387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20388" type="x-p"/> Divide their tongues - Let his counsellors give opposite advice. Let them never agree, and let their devices be confounded. And the prayer was heard. Hushai and Ahithophel gave opposite counsel. Absalom followed that of Hushai; and Ahithophel, knowing that the steps advised by Hushai would bring Absalom's affairs to ruin, went and hanged himself. See 2 Samuel 15, 16, and 17. <div eID="gen20388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20389" type="x-p"/> Violence and strife in the city - They have been concerting violent measures; and thus are full of contention.
entries.61e94fb58569598874803a49e46d47be4163e425: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen20389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20390" type="x-p"/> Day and night they go about - This and the following verse show the state of Jerusalem at this time. Indeed, they exhibit a fair view of the state of any city in the beginning of an insurrection. The leaders are plotting continually; going about to strengthen their party, and to sow new dissensions by misrepresentation, hypocrisy, calumny, and lies.
entries.c74a23c9b33967ecacde28bd5362672b48e731b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen20390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20391" type="x-p"/> It was not an enemy - It is likely that in all these three verses Ahithophel is meant, who, it appears, had been at the bottom of the conspiracy from the beginning; and probably was the first mover of the vain mind of Absalom to do what he did.
entries.3f3d2c9ac759cf91ceb7bd09a86b8956192b1f3a: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen20391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20392" type="x-p"/> Walked unto the house of God in company - Or with haste; for the rabbins teach that we should walk hastily To the temple, but slowly From it.
entries.b715beef3cf2d897a9e0b57806950b71304e7e6a: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen20392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20393" type="x-p"/> Let death seize upon them - This is a prediction of the sudden destruction which should fall on the ringleaders in this rebellion. And it was so. Ahithophel, seeing his counsel rejected, hanged himself. Absalom was defeated; and, fleeing away, he was suspended by the hair in a tree, under which his mule had passed; and being found thus by Joab, he was despatched with three darts; and the people who espoused his interests were almost all cut off. They fell by the sword, or perished in the woods. See <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.8">2Sam 18:8</reference>. <div eID="gen20393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20394" type="x-p"/> Let then go down quick into hell - Let them go down alive into the pit. Let the earth swallow them up! And something of this kind actually took place. Absalom and his army were defeated; twenty thousand of the rebels were slain on the field; and the wood devoured more people that day than the sword devoured, <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.7">2Sam 18:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.8">2Sam 18:8</reference>. The words might be rendered, "Death shall exact upon them; they shall descend alive into sheol." And death did exact his debt upon them, as we have seen above.
entries.331da4a57736ad7ec8e138322aff553dc580d74f: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen20394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20395" type="x-p"/> I will call upon God - He foresaw his deliverance, and the defeat of his enemies and therefore speaks confidently, "The Lord shall save me;" or, as the Targum, "The Word of the Lord shall redeem me."
entries.0b3c8f64eb57ba5142105e539c8ad4763fcb0127: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen20395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20396" type="x-p"/> Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray - This was the custom of the pious Hebrews. See <reference osisRef="Dan.6.10">Dan 6:10</reference>. The Hebrews began their day in the evening, and hence David mentions the evening first. The rabbins say, Men should pray three times each day, because the day changes three times. This was observed in the primitive Church; but the times, in different places, were various. The old Psalter gives this a curious turn: "At even I sall tel his louing (praise) what tim Crist was on the Crosse: and at morn I sall schew his louing, what tim he ros fra dede. And sua he sall here my voyce at mid day, that is sitand at the right hand of his fader, wheder he stegh (ascended) at mid day."
entries.43780e5b9bd5142a6370bf5df79b12dfc74a4087: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen20396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20397" type="x-p"/> He hath delivered my soul - My life he has preserved in perfect safety from the sword; for there were many with me: "for in many afflictions his Word was my support." - Targum. Or David may refer to the supernatural assistance which was afforded him when his enemies were so completely discomfited.
entries.751de0c57dcf791c6b54ca7c00e8f8f8912451e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen20397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20398" type="x-p"/> Because they have no changes - At first Absalom, Ahithophel, and their party, carried all before them. There seemed to be a very general defection of the people; and as in their first attempts they suffered no reverses, therefore they feared not God. Most of those who have few or no afflictions and trials in life, have but little religion. They become sufficient to themselves, and call not upon God.
entries.2f7124ea9629b05b01e5c43f338d20ddfc4ab127: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen20398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20399" type="x-p"/> He hath put forth his hands - A farther description of Ahithophel. He betrayed his friends, and he broke his covenant with his king. He had agreed to serve David for his own emolument, and a stipulation was made accordingly; but while receiving the king's pay, he was endeavoring to subvert the kingdom, and destroy the life of his sovereign.
entries.703756961471efd612d220bdff9d9cf21d12e0aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen20399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20400" type="x-p"/> Were smoother than butter - He was a complete courtier, and a deep, designing hypocrite besides. His words were as soft as butter, and as smooth as oil, while he meditated war; and the fair words which were intended to deceive, were intended also to destroy: they were drawn swords. This is a literal description of the words and conduct of Absalom, as we learn from the inspired historian, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.2">2Sam 15:2</reference>, etc. He was accustomed to wait at the gate; question the persons who came for justice and judgment; throw out broad hints that the king was negligent of the affairs of his kingdom, and had not provided an effective magistracy to administer justice among the people, and added that if he were appointed judge in the land, justice should be done to all. He bowed also to the people, and kissed them; and thus he stole the hearts of the men of Israel. See the passages referred to above.
entries.67e08647dfc4b0699d7cdd37397087c5d3356c41: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen20400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20401" type="x-p"/> Cast thy burden upon the Lord - Whatever cares, afflictions, trials, etc., they may be with which thou art oppressed, lay them upon him. <div eID="gen20401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20402" type="x-p"/> And he shall sustain thee - He shall bear both thee and thy burden. What a glorious promise to a tempted and afflicted soul! God will carry both thee and thy load. Then cast thyself and it upon him. <div eID="gen20402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20403" type="x-p"/> He shall never suffer the righteous to be moved - While a man is righteous, trusts in and depends upon God, he will never suffer him to be shaken. While he trusts in God, and works righteousness, he is as safe as if he were in heaven.
entries.89d18c5c8001e9031de1e87bdd9eba92e85d7dd9: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen20403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20404" type="x-p"/> But thou, O God, shalt bring them down into the pit of destruction - The Chaldee is emphatic: "And thou, O Lord, by thy Word (במימרך bemeymerach) shalt thrust them into the deep gehenna, the bottomless pit, whence they shall never come out; the pit of destruction, where all is amazement, horror, anguish, dismay, ruin, endless loss, and endless suffering." <div eID="gen20404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20405" type="x-p"/> Bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days - So we find, if there be an appointed time to man upon earth, beyond which he cannot pass; yet he may so live as to provoke the justice of God to cut him off before he arrives at that period; yea, before he has reached half way to that limit. According to the decree of God, he might have lived the other half; but he has not done it. <div eID="gen20405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20406" type="x-p"/> But I will trust in thee - Therefore I shall not be moved, and shall live out all the days of my appointed time. <div eID="gen20406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20407" type="x-p"/> The fathers in general apply the principal passages of this Psalm to our Lord's sufferings, the treason of Judas, and the wickedness of the Jews; but these things do not appear to me fairly deducible from the text. It seems to refer plainly enough to the rebellion of Absalom. "The consternation and distress expressed in <reference osisRef="Psa.55.4-Psa.55.8">Psa 55:4-8</reference>, describe the king's state of mind when he fled from Jerusalem, and marched up the mount of Olives, weeping. The iniquity cast upon the psalmist answers to the complaints artfully laid against the king by his son of a negligent administration of justice: and to the reproach of cruelty cast upon him by Shimei, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.2">2Sam 15:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.4">2Sam 15:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.7">2Sam 16:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.8">2Sam 16:8</reference>. The equal, the guide, and the familiar friend, we find in Ahithophel, the confidential counsellor, first of David, afterwards of his son Absalom. The buttery mouth and oily words describe the insidious character of Absalom, as it is delineated, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.5-2Sam.15.9">2Sam 15:5-9</reference>. Still the believer, accustomed to the double edge of the prophetic style, in reading this Psalm, notwithstanding its agreement with the occurrences of David's life, will be led to think of David's great descendant, who endured a bitter agony, and was the victim of a baser treachery, in the same spot where David is supposed to have uttered these complaints." - Bishop Horsley.  <chapter eID="Ps.55"/> <div eID="gen20407" type="x-p"/>

entries.9c1f87eab08960a14899b8416e863a67b0c8dcb8: <div eID="gen9552" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Prayer of One Who Is Maliciously Beset and Betrayed by His Friend</title> <div sID="gen9553" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.54.1-Ps.54.7">Psa 54:1-7</reference> is followed by another Davidic Psalm bearing the same inscription: <hi type="italic">To the Precentor, with accompaniment of stringed instruments, a meditation, by David</hi>. It also accords with the former in the form of the prayer with which it opens (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.55.2">Psa 55:2</reference> with Psa 54:3.); and it is the Elohimic counterpart of the Jahve- <reference osisRef="Ps.41.1">Psa 41:1</reference>-13. If the Psalm is by David, we require (in opposition to Hengstenberg) an assignable occasion for it in the history of his life. For how could the faithless bosom friend, over whom the complaint concerning malicious foes here, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.41.1-Ps.41.13">Psa 41:1-13</reference>, lingers with special sadness, be a mere abstract personage; since it has in the person of Judas Iscariot its historical living antitype in the life and passion of the second David? This Old Testament Judas is none other than Ahithôphel, the right hand of Absalom. Ps 55 belongs, like <reference osisRef="Ps.41.1-Ps.41.13">Psa 41:1-13</reference>, to the four years during which the rebellion of Absalom was forming; only to a somewhat later period, when Absalom’s party were so sure of their cause that they had no need to make any secret of it. How it came to pass that David left the beginnings and progressive steps of the rebellion of Absalom to take their course without bringing any other weapon to bear against it than the weapon of prayer, is discussed on <reference osisRef="Ps.41.1">Psa 41:1</reference>-13. <div eID="gen9553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9554" type="x-p"/> Hitzig also holds this Psalm to be Jeremianic. But it contains no coincidences with the language and thoughts of Jeremiah worth speaking of, excepting that this prophet, in <reference osisRef="Ps.9.1">Psa 9:1</reference>, gives utterance to a similar wish to that of the psalmist in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.7">Psa 55:7</reference>, and springing from the same motive. The argument in favour of Jeremiah in opposition to David is consequently referred to the picture of life and suffering which is presented in the Psalm; and it becomes a question whether this harmonizes better with the persecuted life of Jeremiah or of David. The exposition which follows here places itself - and it is at least worthy of being attempted - on the standpoint of the writer of the inscription. <div eID="gen9554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9555" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.55.1-Ps.55.8">Psa 55:1-8</reference> <div eID="gen9555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9556" type="x-p"/> In this first group sorrow prevails. David spreads forth his deep grief before God, and desires for himself some lonely spot in the wilderness far away from the home or lurking-place of the confederate band of those who are compassing his overthrow. “Veil not Thyself” here, where what is spoken of is something audible, not visible, is equivalent to “veil not Thine ear,” <reference osisRef="Lam.3.56">Lam 3:56</reference>, which He designedly does, when the right state of heart leaves the praying one, and consequently that which makes it acceptable and capable of being answered is wanting to the prayer (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Isa 1:15</reference>). שׂיח signifies a shrub (Syriac <hi type="italic">shucho</hi>, Arabic <hi type="italic">šı̂ḥ</hi>), and also reflection and care (Arabic, carefulness, attention; Aramaic, סח, to babble, talk, discourse). The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. חריד, which in <reference osisRef="Gen.27.40">Gen 27:40</reference> signifies to lead a roving life, has in this instance the signification to move one’s self backwards and forwards, to be inwardly uneasy; root רד, Arab. <hi type="italic">rd</hi>, to totter, whence <hi type="italic">râda , jarûda</hi>, to run up and down (IV to desire, will); <hi type="italic">raida</hi>, to shake (said of a soft bloated body); <hi type="italic">radda</hi>, to turn (whence <hi type="italic">taraddud</hi>, a moving to and fro, doubting); therefore: I wander hither and thither in my reflecting or meditating, turning restlessly from one thought to another. It is not necessary to read ואחמיה after <reference osisRef="Ps.77.4">Psa 77:4</reference> instead of ועהימה, since the verb הוּם = המה, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.6">Psa 42:6</reference>, 12, is secured by the derivatives. Since these only exhibit הוּם, and not הים (in Arabic used more particularly of the raving of love), ואהימה, as also אריד, is <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>., and in fact like this latter used with an inward object: I am obliged to raise a tumult or groan, break out into the dull murmuring sounds of pain. The cohortative not unfrequently signifies “I have to” or “I must” of incitements within one’s self which are under the control of outward circumstances. In this restless state of mind he finds himself, and he is obliged to break forth into this cry of pain on account of the voice of the foe which he cannot but hear; by reason of the pressure or constraint (עקת) of the evil-doer which he is compelled to feel. The conjecture צעקת (Olshausen and Hupfeld) is superfluous. עקה is a more elegant Aramaizing word instead of צרה. <div eID="gen9556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9557" type="x-p"/> The second strophe begins with a more precise statement of that which justifies his pain. The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. חמיט signifies here, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.140.11">Psa 140:11</reference> (<hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>), <hi type="italic">declinare</hi>: they cast or roll down evil (calamity) upon him and maliciously lay snares for him בּאף, breathing anger against him who is conscious of having manifested only love towards them. His heart turns about in his body, it writhes (יהיל); cf. on this, Psa 38:11. Fear and trembling take possession of his inward parts; יבא in the expression יבא בי, as is always the case when followed by a tone syllable, is a so-called נסוג אחור, i.e., it has the tone that has retreated to the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.38">Deu 1:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.7.24">Isa 7:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.20">Isa 60:20</reference>), although this is only with difficulty discernible in our printed copies, and is therefore (vid., <hi type="italic">Accentsystem</hi>, vi. §2) noted with <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>. The <hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>. which follows introduces the heightened state of terror which proceeds from this crowding on of fear and trembling. Moreover, the wish that is thereby urged from him, which David uttered to himself, is introduced in the third strophe by a <hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi> (Note: That beautiful old song of the church concerning Jesus has grown out of this strophe: -<hi type="italic">Ecquis binas columbinas Alas dabit animae? Et in almam crucis palmam Evolat citissime</hi>, etc.) “Who will give me?” is equivalent to “Oh that I had!” Ges. §136, 1. In ואשׁכּנה is involved the self-satisfying signification of settling down (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.13">Eze 31:13</reference>), of coming to rest and remaining in a place (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.10">2Sa 7:10</reference>). Without going out of our way, a sense perfectly in accordance with the matter in hand may be obtained for אחישׁה מפלט לי, if אחישׁה is taken not as <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.12">Psa 71:12</reference>), but after <reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">Isa 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.12">Isa 60:12</reference>, as <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>.: I would hasten, i.e., quickly find for myself a place which might serve me as a shelter from the raging wind, from the storm. רוּח סעה is equivalent to the Arabic <hi type="italic">rihin sâijat - in</hi>, inasmuch as Arab. <hi type="italic">s‛â</hi>, “to move one’s self quickly, to go or run swiftly,” can be said both of light (Koran, 66:8) and of water-brooks (vid., Jones, <hi type="italic">Comm. Poes. Asiat., ed. Lipsiae</hi>, p. 358), and also of strong currents of air, of winds, and such like. The correction סערה, proposed by Hupfeld, produces a disfiguring tautology. Among those about David there is a wild movement going on which is specially aimed at his overthrow. From this he would gladly flee and hide himself, like a dove taking refuge in a cleft of the rock from the approaching storm, or from the talons of the bird of prey, fleeing with its noiseless but persevering flight.<note placement="foot">Kimchi observes that the dove, when she becomes tired, draws in one wing and flies with the other, and thus the more surely escapes. Aben-Ezra finds an allusion here to the carrier-pigeon.</note>
entries.4f09a7f8fb5b77662708f4fb23f12a5d53e6e655: <reference osisRef="Ps.55.9-Ps.55.16">Psa 55:9-16</reference> <div eID="gen9557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9558" type="x-p"/> In the second group anger is the prevailing feeling. In the city all kinds of party passions have broken loose; even his bosom friend has taken a part in this hostile rising. The retrospective reference to the confusion of tongues at Babel which is contained in the word פּלּג (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.10.25">Gen 10:25</reference>), also in remembrance of בּלל (<reference osisRef="Gen.11.1-Gen.11.9">Gen 11:1-9</reference>), involves the choice of the word בּלּע, which here, after <reference osisRef="Isa.19.3">Isa 19:3</reference>, denotes a swallowing up, i.e., annihilation by means of confounding and rendering utterly futile. לשׁונם is the object to both imperatives, the second of which is פּלּג (like the pointing usual in connection with a final guttural) for the sake of similarity of sound. Instead of חמס וריב, the pointing is חמס וריב, which is perfectly regular, because the וריב with a conjunctive accent logically hurries on to בּעיר as its supplement.<note placement="foot">Certain exceptions, however, exist, inasmuch as ו sometimes remains even in connection with a disjunctive accent, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Isa 49:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.40.10">Jer 40:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.41.16">Jer 41:16</reference>; and it is pointed ו in connection with a conjunctive in <reference osisRef="Gen.45.23">Gen 45:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.46.12">Gen 46:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.9.3">Lev 9:3</reference>; Mic 2:11; <reference osisRef="Job.4.16">Job 4:16</reference>; Ecc 4:8.</note> <div eID="gen9558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9559" type="x-p"/> The subjects to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.55.11">Psa 55:11</reference></hi> are not violence and strife (Hengstenberg, Hitzig), for it is rather a comical idea to make these personified run round about upon the city walls; but (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.59.7">Psa 59:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.15">Psa 59:15</reference>) the Absalomites, and in fact the spies who incessantly watch the movements of David and his followers, and who to this end roam about upon the heights of the city. The narrative in 2 Sam. 15 shows how passively David looked on at this movement, until he abandoned the palace of his own free will and quitted Jerusalem  The espionage in the circuit of the city is contrasted with the movements going on within the city itself by the word בּקרב. We are acquainted with but few details of the affair; but we can easily fill in the details for ourselves in accordance with the ambitious, base, and craftily malicious character of Absalom. The assertion that deceit (מרמה) and the extremest madness had taken possession of the city is confirmed in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.13">Psa 55:13</reference> by כּי. It is not open enemies who might have had cause for it that are opposed to him, but faithless friends, and among them that Ahithophel of Giloh, the scum of perfidious ingratitude. The futures ואשּׂא and ואסּתר are used as subjunctives, and ו is equivalent to <hi type="italic">alioqui</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.51.18">Psa 51:18</reference>, cf. Job 6:14. He tells him to his face, to his shame, the relationship in which he had stood to him whom he now betrays. <reference osisRef="Ps.55.14">Psa 55:14</reference> is not to be rendered: and thou art, etc., but: <hi type="italic">and thou</hi> (who dost act thus) <hi type="italic">wast</hi>, etc.; for it is only because the principal clause has a retrospective meaning that the futures נמתּיק and נהלּך describe what was a custom in the past. The expression is designedly אנושׁ כּערכּי and not אישׁ כערכי; David does not make him feel his kingly eminence, but places himself in the relation to him of man to man, putting him on the same level with himself and treating him as his equal. The suffix of כערכי is in this instance not subjective as in the כערכך of the law respecting the <hi type="italic">asham</hi> or trespass-offering: according to my estimation, but objectively: equal to the worth at which I am estimated, that is to say, equally valued with myself. What heart-piercing significance this word obtains when found in the mouth of the second David, who, although the Son of God and peerless King, nevertheless entered into the most intimate human relationship as the Son of man to His disciples, and among them to that Iscariot! אלּוּף from אלף, Arabic <hi type="italic">alifa</hi>, to be accustomed to anything, <hi type="italic">assuescere</hi>, signifies one attached to or devoted to any one; and מידּא, according to the Hebrew meaning of the verb ידע, an intimate acquaintance. The first of the relative clauses in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.15">Psa 55:15</reference> describes their confidential private intercourse; the second the unrestrained manifestation of it in public. סוד here, as in <reference osisRef="Job.19.19">Job 19:19</reference> (vid., <hi type="italic">supra</hi> on <reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Psa 25:14</reference>). המתּיק סוד, to make friendly intercourse sweet, is equivalent to cherishing it. רגשׁ stands over against סוד, just like סוד, secret counsel, and רגשׁה, loud tumult, in Psa 64:3. Here רגשׁ is just the same as that which the Korahitic poet calls המון חוגג in Psa 42:5. <div eID="gen9559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9560" type="x-p"/> In the face of the faithless friends who has become the head of the Absalomite faction David now breaks out, in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.16">Psa 55:16</reference>, into fearful imprecations. The <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> is ישׁימות, <hi type="italic">desolationes</hi> (<hi type="italic">super eos</hi>); but this word occurs only in the name of a place (“House of desolations”), and does not well suit such direct reference to persons. On the other hand, the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> ישּׁיאמות, let death ensnare or impose upon them, gives a sense that is not to be objected to; it is a pregnant expression, equivalent to: let death come upon them unexpectedly. To this ישּׁיא corresponds the חיּים of the second imprecation: let them go down alive into Hades (שׁאול, perhaps originally שׁאולה, the ה of which may have been lost beside the ח that follows), i.e., like the company of Korah, while their life is yet vigorous, that is to say, let them die a sudden, violent death. The drawing together of the <hi type="italic">decipiat (opprimat) mors</hi> into one word is the result of the ancient <hi type="italic">scriptio continua</hi> and of the defective mode of writing, ישּׁי, like יני, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.5">Psa 141:5</reference>, אבי, 1Ki 21:29. Böttcher renders it differently: let death crash in upon them; but the future form ישּׁי = ישׁאה from שׁאה = שׁאי is an imaginary one, which cannot be supported by Num 21:30. Hitzig renders it: let death benumb them (ישּׁים); but this gives an inconceivable figure, with the turgidity of which the <hi type="italic">trepidantes Manes</hi> in Virgil, <hi type="italic">Aenid</hi> viii. 246, do not admit of comparison. In the confirmation, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.55.16">Psa 55:16</reference></hi>, בּמגוּרם, together with the בּקרבּם which follows, does not pretend to be any advance in the thought, whether מגור be rendered a settlement, dwelling, παροικία (lxx, Targum), or an assembly (Aquila, Symmachus, Jerome). Hence Hitzig’s rendering: in their shrine, in their breast (= ἐν τῷ θησαυρῷ τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν, <reference osisRef="Luke.6.45">Luk 6:45</reference>), מגוּרם being short for מגוּרתם in accordance with the love of contraction which prevails in poetry (on <reference osisRef="Ps.25.5">Psa 25:5</reference>). But had the poet intended to use this figure he would have written בּמגוּרת קרבם, and is not the assertion that wickedness is among them, that it is at home in them, really a climax? The change of the names of God in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.17">Psa 55:17</reference> is significant. He calls upon Him who is exalted above the world, and He who mercifully interposes in the history of the world helps him.
entries.f70f121cd37147bb0af7ef47ab80ed893e6468dc: <reference osisRef="Ps.55.17-Ps.55.23">Psa 55:17-23</reference> <div eID="gen9560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9561" type="x-p"/> In the third group confidence prevails, the tone that is struck up in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.17">Psa 55:17</reference> being carried forward. Evening morning, and noon, as the beginning, middle, and close of the day, denote the day in its whole compass or extent: David thus gives expression to the incessancy with which he is determined to lay before God, both in the quiet of his spirit and in louder utterances, whatsoever moves him. The <hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>. ויּשׁמע connects the hearing (answer) with the prayer as its inevitable result. Also in the <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. פּדה expression is given to the certainty of faith; and בּשׁלום side by side with it denotes, with the same pregnancy of meaning as in <reference osisRef="Ps.118.5">Psa 118:5</reference>, the state of undisturbed outward and inward safety and prosperity, into which God removes his soul when He rescues him. If we read <hi type="italic">mi - kerob</hi>, then קרב is, as the ancient versions regard it, the infinitive: <hi type="italic">ne</hi> <hi type="italic">appropinquent mihi</hi>; whereas since the time of J. H. Michaelis the preference has been given to the pronunciation <hi type="italic">mi - kerāb</hi>: <hi type="italic">a conflictu mihi sc. parato</hi>, in which case it would be pointed מקּרב־ (with <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>), whilst the MSS, in order to guard against the reading with <hi type="italic">ā</hi>, point it מקּרב־. Hitzig is right when he observes, that after the negative מן the infinitive is indicated beforehand, and that לי = עלי, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.2">Psa 27:2</reference>, is better suited to this. Moreover, the confirmatory clause <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.55.19">Psa 55:19</reference></hi> is connected with what precedes in a manner less liable to be misunderstood if מקרב is taken as infinitive: that they may not be able to gain any advantage over me, cannot come near me to harm me (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.10">Psa 91:10</reference>). For it is not until now less precarious to take the enemies as the subject of היוּ, and to take עמּדי in a hostile sense, as in <reference osisRef="Job.10.17">Job 10:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.19">Job 13:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.13">Job 31:13</reference>, cf. עם <reference osisRef="Ps.94.16">Psa 94:16</reference>, and this is only possible where the connection suggests this sense. Heidenheim’s interpretation: among the magnates were those who succoured me (viz., Hushai, Zadok, and Abiathar, by whom the counsel of Athithopel was frustrated), does not give a thought characteristic of the Psalms. And with Aben-Ezra, who follows <hi type="italic">Numeri Rabba</hi> 294 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, to think of the assistance of angels in connection with בּרבּים, certainly strongly commends itself in view of 2Ki 6:16 (with which Hitzig also compares <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.7">2Ch 32:7</reference>); here, however, it has no connection, whereas the thought, “as many (consisting of many) are they with me, i.e., do they come forward and fight with me,” is very loosely attached to what has gone before.
